did_you_know.text: Did you know? The psalm begins with performance instructions: it is intended for the director of music, attributed to the sons of Korah, and described as a “maskil”—a song with instructive content—and as a “song of love.”
Did you know? The poet describes his song as if it arises spontaneously: his heart overflows with a good theme, and his tongue is like the pen of a skillful writer.
Did you know? The king is praised in this verse for three things: his beauty, the graciousness of his speech, and the divine blessing that rests on him forever.

Did you know? The king does not go to war merely for his own power; he is portrayed as riding forth “for truth, humility, and righteousness”—expressions that connect his rule with truth, humility, and justice.
Did you know? The verse presents the king’s throne as stable and everlasting, and calls the scepter of his kingdom a “scepter of righteousness”—a symbol of fairness and uprightness.
Did you know? Justice is central to the king’s character: he loves righteousness and hates wickedness, and is therefore described as anointed with the oil of joy.
Did you know? The king’s portrayal now shifts from that of a mighty warrior to that of a splendid bridegroom: his garments are perfumed, and he comes from ivory palaces amid joyful celebration.
Did you know? The queen is presented standing at the king’s right hand, dressed in gold from Ophir; princesses are also mentioned, honoring the royal occasion.
Did you know? The bride is called to listen, look, and pay attention, and to forget her people and her father’s house—a picture of her entering her new position beside the king.
Did you know? Tyre is mentioned as the source of a gift for the bride, along with the wealthiest people; this shows the honor that the royal wedding inspires even beyond the king’s court.

Did you know? The psalm’s conclusion links the continuation of the royal line with the remembrance of the king’s name: his sons will become princes, and the poet promises to make his name remembered from generation to generation, so that the nations will praise him forever.
